target.title: Combining Residual Networks with LSTMs for Lipreading
target.version: ISCA Interspeech 2017 proceedings paper; version label not stated on the first page

read.pdf: Fig. 1–3 captions/descriptions and Tables 1–6 read in text.txt; PDF itself not supplied

target.first_public_note: arXiv:1703.04105 v1 (2017-03) precedes the Interspeech 2017 proceedings (2017-08); the ISCA version was read, arXiv v4 consulted for the 74.2/76.2 discrepancy.

entries.text: The proposed visual speech recognizer combines a spatiotemporal convolutional front-end, a ResNet, and a bidirectional LSTM back-end in an end-to-end architecture.
entries.condition: Visual-only word-level lipreading on LRW.
entries.quote: The system is a combination of spatiotemporal convolutional, residual and bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory networks.

entries.text: The authors characterize the system as implicit keyword spotting because the target word occurs inside an utterance rather than an isolated clip.
entries.condition: Fixed-duration LRW excerpts; word boundaries are not supplied to the model.

entries.text: The LRW task has 500 target-word classes.
entries.condition: LRW visual word recognition; each clip is labeled by its target word.

entries.text: Each LRW clip is 1.28 seconds long and contains 31 frames at 25 fps.
entries.condition: LRW video excerpts used for training, validation, and evaluation.

entries.text: The training split contains up to 1,000 occurrences per target word; validation and evaluation each contain 50 occurrences per word.
entries.unit: clips per target word in train; validation; evaluation
entries.condition: Official LRW word-class splits; speaker/session overlap between splits is not reported.

entries.text: The LRW evaluation set contains 25,000 clips in total.
entries.condition: 50 evaluation clips for each of 500 target words; word accuracy is reported.
entries.quote: Recall that the number of evaluation clips is 50 per target word (i.e. 25000 clips overall).

entries.text: No word-boundary information is used during training or evaluation.
entries.condition: LRW clips contain target words within longer utterances.

entries.text: The authors describe LRW as approximately 500,000 clips with speaker, pose, and illumination variability and in-the-wild recording conditions.
entries.condition: LRW dataset; BBC TV broadcast-derived visual speech clips.

entries.text: The authors state that the word-label architecture could also support viseme recognition by replacing word labels with viseme labels at the SoftMax layer; this was not the reported evaluation task.
entries.condition: The reported experiments use 500 LRW word labels.

entries.text: Preprocessing uses 66 facial landmarks to crop and resize frames to 112×112 pixels.
entries.condition: A shared crop is applied across all frames in each clip using median landmark coordinates.

entries.text: Training augmentation uses random crop offsets of ±5 pixels and horizontal flips shared across the clip's frames.
entries.condition: Training only; the same crop and flip are applied across a given clip's frames.
entries.quote: Finally, data augmentation is performed during training, by ap- plying random cropping (±5 pixels) and horizontal ﬂips, that are common across all frames of a given clip.

entries.text: Frames are converted to grayscale and normalized using an overall mean and variance; the paper does not report the numerical statistics or their estimation subset.
entries.condition: Visual input preprocessing for all clips.

entries.text: The 3D spatiotemporal front-end uses 64 kernels of size 5×7×7.
entries.condition: Visual LRW input; the kernel dimensions are time/width/height.

entries.text: The spatiotemporal front-end has approximately 16,000 parameters.
entries.condition: 3D convolutional front-end for LRW visual input.

entries.text: The framewise image encoder is the 34-layer identity-mapping ResNet.
entries.condition: ResNet applied to each time step.
entries.quote: We use the 34-layer identity- mapping version, which was proposed for ImageNet, [31].

entries.text: The ResNet has approximately 21 million parameters.
entries.condition: 34-layer ResNet applied to each time step.

entries.text: The authors did not initialize from pretrained models, stating that ImageNet/CIFAR models were optimized for different tasks.
entries.condition: Training of the reported LRW ResNet.

entries.text: The back-end stacks two LSTMs in each direction of a bidirectional network and has approximately 2.4 million parameters.
entries.condition: Forward and backward final-layer outputs are concatenated in the proposed N7 system.
entries.quote: For each of the two directions, we stack two LSTMs, and the outputs of the ﬁnal LSTMs are concatenated.

entries.text: The LSTM back-end has approximately 2.4 million parameters.
entries.condition: Two-layer bidirectional LSTM back-end.

entries.text: The word label is repeated at every time step, and the loss aggregates the negative log word posteriors across all time steps.
entries.condition: Word-level supervision; word boundaries are unknown and not used.

entries.text: Applying the word criterion at every time step reportedly improved word accuracy by about 3 percentage points over applying it only at the final LSTM time step.
entries.condition: Comparison of two word-level loss placements after experimentation; LRW task.

entries.text: The paper reports SGD with momentum 0.9.
entries.condition: Reported optimization/training configuration for the paper's models.

entries.text: Batch normalization follows convolutional and linear layers except for the layer immediately before SoftMax.
entries.condition: Network training configuration.

entries.text: The paper reports no dropout.
entries.condition: Network training configuration; the authors say batch normalization seemed sufficient.

entries.text: The reported learning rate decreases logarithmically from 5×10⁻⁴ to 5×10⁻⁵.
entries.condition: Training configuration; schedule decreases on a log scale.

entries.text: Training completion is monitored on the validation set with a three-epoch delay; the paper does not name the monitored metric in this stopping sentence.
entries.condition: Validation-set stopping/monitoring during training.

entries.text: The authors report convergence after 15–20 epochs.
entries.condition: Reported across the models; no seed-wise variability or repetitions are given.

entries.text: Training uses a temporal-convolution initialization stage, then a five-epoch Bi-LSTM initialization with the front-end and ResNet frozen, followed by end-to-end training.
entries.condition: Three-stage training recipe; the 3D front-end and ResNet are fixed during Bi-LSTM initialization.
entries.quote: The Bi-LSTM is trained for 5 epochs, keeping the weights of the 3D convolution front-end and the ResNet ﬁxed.

entries.text: The cited LipNet work reports 95.2% sentence-level accuracy on a subset of GRID speakers, trained using the remaining GRID speakers. (as reported by the target)
entries.condition: GRID; held-out subset of speakers for evaluation and remaining speakers for training; this is sentence-level, not LRW word-level recognition.

entries.text: The cited visual-only WAS system is reported at 97.0% on GRID and 74.2% on LRW. (as reported by the target)
entries.unit: % Top-1 word accuracy on GRID; % Top-1 word accuracy on LRW
entries.condition: Visual-only WAS; pretrained on BBC TV broadcasts and fine-tuned on the GRID and LRW training sets; the paper gives no speaker-overlap, seed, or decoding details for this comparison.
entries.quote: Word accuracies (Top-1) equal to 97.0% and 74.2% are reported on GRID and LRW respectively

entries.text: Elsewhere, the paper gives the LRW state-of-the-art comparator as 76.2% and says the proposed 83.0% result improves on it by 6.8 percentage points. (as reported by the target)
entries.unit: % LRW word accuracy (Top-1), as cited by the target paper
entries.condition: The target paper attributes this result to an attentional encoder-decoder; it is inconsistent with the 74.2% LRW figure in Sec. 5.1.
entries.quote: 6.8% absolute improvement over the state-of-the- art 76.2% accuracy

entries.text: The published multi-tower VGG-M baseline is reported at 61.1% Top-1 and 90.4% Top-10 word accuracy. (as reported by the target)
entries.condition: LRW baseline result attributed to [4]; 500-word task; exact seed, speaker partition details, and decoder are not restated in this paper.

entries.text: N1 reports 69.6% / 90.4% / 94.8% Top-1 / Top-5 / Top-10 word accuracy.
entries.condition: LRW evaluation split; 500 classes and 50 clips per word (25,000 total); N1 uses 2D convolution, ResNet, and temporal-convolution back-end; no boundaries; speaker overlap, repetitions/seeds, and LM/decoder details are unreported.

entries.text: N2 reports 74.6% / 93.4% / 96.5% Top-1 / Top-5 / Top-10 word accuracy.
entries.condition: LRW evaluation split; 500 classes and 50 clips per word (25,000 total); N2 uses 3D convolution, ResNet, and temporal-convolution back-end; no boundaries; speaker overlap, repetitions/seeds, and LM/decoder details are unreported.

entries.text: N3 reports 69.7% / 90.5% / 94.6% Top-1 / Top-5 / Top-10 word accuracy.
entries.condition: LRW evaluation split; 500 classes and 50 clips per word (25,000 total); N3 substitutes a roughly parameter-matched three-layer DNN for ResNet; no boundaries; speaker overlap, repetitions/seeds, and LM/decoder details are unreported.

entries.text: N4 reports 78.4% / 94.9% / 97.4% Top-1 / Top-5 / Top-10 word accuracy.
entries.condition: LRW evaluation split; 500 classes and 50 clips per word (25,000 total); N4 uses a single-layer Bi-LSTM initialized from N2 with the front-end and ResNet frozen; no boundaries; speaker overlap, repetitions/seeds, and LM/decoder details are unreported.

entries.text: N5 reports 79.6% / 95.3% / 96.3% Top-1 / Top-5 / Top-10 word accuracy.
entries.condition: LRW evaluation split; 500 classes and 50 clips per word (25,000 total); N5 uses a two-layer Bi-LSTM initialized from N2 with the front-end and ResNet frozen; directional outputs are added; no boundaries; speaker overlap, repetitions/seeds, and LM/decoder details are unreported.

entries.text: N6 reports 81.5% / 96.0% / 98.0% Top-1 / Top-5 / Top-10 word accuracy.
entries.condition: LRW evaluation split; 500 classes and 50 clips per word (25,000 total); N6 is end-to-end fine-tuning of N5 and adds the two directional LSTM outputs; no boundaries; speaker overlap, repetitions/seeds, and LM/decoder details are unreported.

entries.text: N7, the proposed end-to-end model with concatenated directional LSTM outputs, reports 83.0% / 96.3% / 98.3% Top-1 / Top-5 / Top-10 word accuracy.
entries.condition: LRW evaluation split; 500 classes and 50 clips per word (25,000 total); no word boundaries; speaker overlap, repetitions/seeds, and LM/decoder details are unreported.

entries.text: The authors report an 8.5-percentage-point Top-1 gain for N1 over the published VGG-M baseline.
entries.unit: percentage points in Top-1 word accuracy
entries.condition: LRW; N1 69.6% versus VGG-M 61.1%; Table 1 and Table 2 results.

entries.text: Replacing 2D with 3D convolution improves Top-1 accuracy by 5.0 percentage points in the N1–N2 comparison.
entries.unit: percentage points in Top-1 word accuracy
entries.condition: LRW; N1 2D front-end at 69.6% versus N2 3D front-end at 74.6%; temporal-convolution back-end held constant.
entries.quote: the use of 3D (N2) instead of 2D (N1) leads to a further 5.0% absolute improvement

entries.text: The ResNet is reported to outperform a roughly parameter-matched three-layer DNN by 4.9 percentage points in word accuracy.
entries.unit: percentage points in Top-1 word accuracy
entries.condition: LRW; N2 ResNet 74.6% versus N3 DNN 69.7%; DNN has approximately the same parameter count.

entries.text: Using a single-layer Bi-LSTM instead of temporal convolution is reported to improve Top-1 accuracy by 3.8 percentage points.
entries.unit: percentage points in Top-1 word accuracy
entries.condition: LRW; N4 78.4% versus N2 74.6%; front-end and ResNet held fixed, with N4 back-end trained from N2 weights.
entries.quote: by using a single-layer Bi-LSTM (N4) instead of a temporal convolutional back-end, a further 3.8% absolute improvement is attained

entries.text: Using a two-layer rather than single-layer Bi-LSTM is reported to add 1.2 percentage points in Top-1 accuracy.
entries.unit: percentage points in Top-1 word accuracy
entries.condition: LRW; N5 79.6% versus N4 78.4%; both initialized from N2 with the front-end and ResNet frozen.

entries.text: End-to-end training of N5 is reported to add 1.9 percentage points in Top-1 accuracy.
entries.unit: percentage points in Top-1 word accuracy
entries.condition: LRW; N6 81.5% versus N5 79.6%; end-to-end stage starts from N5 weights.
entries.quote: By training N5 in an end-to-end fashion (N6) we obtain a 1.9% absolute improvement

entries.text: Concatenating rather than adding the two directional LSTM outputs gives the best reported result, N7.
entries.condition: LRW; N7 uses concatenation and N6 uses addition; the table reports 83.0% versus 81.5% Top-1.

entries.text: The abstract claims 83.0% word accuracy and a 6.8-percentage-point absolute improvement over the current state of the art.
entries.unit: % word accuracy; percentage points over claimed state of the art
entries.condition: LRW word-level evaluation without word-boundary information; the comparison baseline is inconsistent within the paper (74.2% in Sec. 5.1 versus 76.2% in Sec. 6).
entries.quote: The proposed network attains word accu- racy equal to 83.0%, yielding 6.8% absolute improvement over the current state-of-the-art, without using information about word boundaries during training or testing.

entries.text: The conclusion claims the 83.0% result is less than half the baseline VGG-M error rate.
entries.condition: LRW Top-1 comparison: proposed N7 versus VGG-M baseline; the paper phrases this as a relative error-rate claim.

entries.text: The authors note that clips include coarticulation from adjacent words, making the first and last visemes of the target word occasionally difficult to identify.
entries.condition: LRW evaluation clips are excerpts from continuous speech and target words are not isolated.
entries.quote: We should emphasize again that the clips contain coarticulation with preceding and succeeding words, as they are excerpted from continuous speech.

entries.text: The authors explicitly concede that identifying a target word's first and last visemes is occasionally hard.
entries.condition: Coarticulated LRW clips from continuous speech.

entries.text: The paper gives no speaker counts, identities, or evidence that speakers are disjoint across LRW train, validation, and evaluation splits.

entries.quote: Training is considered complete when the results on the valida- tion set do no longer improve, with a delay of 3 epochs.

entries.text: The paper does not give numeric normalization mean/variance values or state the data subset used to estimate them.
entries.condition: The text only says normalization uses overall mean and variance; exact computation provenance is absent.

entries.text: No chance-level or chance-corrected comparison is reported for the 500-class word-recognition evaluation.

entries.text: The paper does not specify an external language model, lexicon, beam search, or other separate decoding aid for the reported LRW evaluation.
entries.condition: The architecture applies SoftMax at each time step; no separate use-time language aid is described.

entries.text: No user confirmation or accept/reject step is described; the evaluation is automatic word classification scored by Top-N accuracy.
entries.condition: Benchmark evaluation rather than an interactive user study.

entries.text: No user correction mechanism or post-recognition editing procedure is described.
entries.condition: The reported task is offline LRW word recognition; no interactive correction protocol is given.

entries.text: Training is reported on a single NVIDIA Titan X GPU with 12 GB memory.
entries.condition: Paper implementation hardware; the paper does not report inference latency or throughput.

entries.text: No real-time latency, throughput, or deployment evaluation is reported.
entries.condition: The paper reports training hardware only, not end-user or streaming performance.

entries.text: The linked Torch repository sets a default manual seed of 1 and seeds both Torch and all CUDA devices; data-loader workers use manualSeed + worker index.
entries.condition: Code-only reproducibility setting; the paper gives no seed or repetition details.

entries.text: The repository normalizes byte images by dividing by 255, then subtracting mean 0.4161 and dividing by standard deviation 0.1688; its comment says these statistics came from a very small subset of training images.
entries.condition: Code-only numeric normalization and estimation subset; the paper gives no numeric values or subset provenance.

entries.text: The repository applies a horizontal flip with probability 0.5 during training; the paper reports flips but not their probability.
entries.condition: Training augmentation; applied consistently across frames in a clip.

entries.text: The repository's training loop saves the best checkpoint by validation Top-1 error; the paper says validation controls completion but does not give this exact metric/checkpoint rule.
entries.condition: Validation split is used for model selection in the code; best model is saved when testTop1 improves.

entries.text: In test-only mode the repository hard-codes the checkpoint filename model_19.t7; the paper does not identify the final evaluation checkpoint.
entries.condition: Repository test-only path; this should not be conflated with the separately saved best validation checkpoint.

entries.text: The repository's validation/test preprocessing uses a center crop; ten-crop evaluation defaults to false and is only enabled for validation in the data loader.
entries.condition: Current repository preprocessing; paper describes landmark-based common cropping and does not specify this exact evaluation crop switch.

entries.text: The repository ranks test predictions by summing per-time-step output scores; its example evaluator averages framewise log-posteriors. The paper does not specify the test-time aggregation rule.
entries.value: sum in trainer; mean in example evaluator
entries.condition: Code-only decoding detail; no external language model is used in these script paths.

questions.q: What exactly does the headline 83.0% result establish, and under what benchmark conditions?
questions.answer: It is Top-1 word accuracy for 500-way visual word recognition on LRW's 25,000-clip evaluation split, with 50 clips per word and no word-boundary information. The paper does not report speaker/session overlap, seed repetitions, chance level, or an external LM; the repository adds code-only seed, normalization, checkpoint, and crop details.

questions.q: How reliable is the paper's claimed 6.8-point state-of-the-art margin?
questions.answer: The 6.8-point claim compares 83.0% with 76.2%, but Sec. 5.1 reports 74.2% for LRW WAS; the paper does not reconcile these figures. It also omits several reproducibility details for the comparison, including seeds and speaker overlap.

questions.q: Which architectural choices are supported by the ablations?
questions.answer: The reported comparisons favor 3D over 2D convolution, ResNet over a parameter-matched DNN, Bi-LSTM over temporal convolution, two LSTM layers over one, end-to-end fine-tuning, and concatenating rather than adding directional outputs.

questions.q: What main task limitations do the authors acknowledge?
questions.answer: Target words remain embedded in continuous utterances, so coarticulation makes boundary visemes difficult; accuracy also varies sharply across the 500 target words.
